doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

chapter: Kai and J.J., Bohemia and Embers
title: Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson group
summary: Working with Kai and J.J., six albums for Columbia, their contrasting styles and the last gig at Newport 1956.

bands.name: Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson group

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Well I used to work, okay I’ll get back to me chronologically. So after Tony Scott I started working with Kai Winding and J.J. Johnson. Kai and Jay. Very successful. The most successful commercial group I’d ever — he had some hit records. And the group was a great experience because it was very tightly organized. And I made about six albums with them. I’m still waiting for them to be on CD. We recorded for Columbia with Paul Chambers and Kenny Clarke and I was spoiled that way. Even now, like because I played with all these great people, like if I get a group now and like drummers, some of them are great but you can’t get them and I’m not in a position to do that although a recent gig I had at the Charlie Parker Festival I played with one of the young drummers who I think would have more than held his own in the old days, his name is Lewis Nash. He’s really terrific. He’s great. And George Mraz is George Mraz. But what was I saying just before that?
We were talking about the group with J.J. and Kai.

Oh. J.J. and Kai. We traveled a lot and we had records and it was a remarkable group because of how well they organized it. J.J. was — they were very different. Even — they played similarly but not, they’re really different if you listen. J.J. was smooth, controlled and Kai was sort of brash. But they were in the idiom and they were great foils for each other and they devised all these arrangements with mutes and everything. It was a terrific experience. And our last gig was at the 1956 Newport festival and we went in the studio and made one more album and then they went their separate ways and J.J. had this great successful career and Kai, Kai interestingly wanted to get out of jazz. He wanted money. So he started — a lot of critics, they just don’t get it. They think that just ‘cause you play great you’re not entitled to make a lot of money.
